title: A Civilian Plane Crashed in New Mexico. Was the Military’s Tech to Blame?
gist: A medevac King Air crashed into the Capitan Mountains near Ruidoso, New Mexico on May 14 after an Air Force NAVFEST GPS-jamming exercise at White Sands left the crew — and aircraft for hundreds of miles — without satellite navigation, the first US civilian fatal crash linked to electronic warfare. The article argues counter-drone electronic warfare is colliding with a civil aviation system that remains heavily GPS-dependent and very slow to adapt, with a Pakistani 737 freighter crash near the jamming-saturated Strait of Hormuz as a possible next data point.

insights.claim: US military personnel conducting a GPS jamming exercise at the White Sands Missile Range left a medevac King Air crew — and any other aircraft within hundreds of miles — unable to use modern navigation, forcing a reversion to older technology the pilots rarely used before they became disoriented and hit a mountain, killing all four aboard.
insights.speaker: Jeff Wise
insights.so_what: Establishes a direct, attributable civilian-casualty cost of domestic electronic warfare testing — the precondition for regulatory or liability change.
insights.locator: But once airborne, the plane ran into trouble

insights.claim: The 746th Test Squadron of the 704th Test Group holds NAVFEST annually at White Sands, drawing electronic warfare units from across the armed services for two weeks of testing GPS disruption and counter-disruption technology.
insights.speaker: Jeff Wise
insights.so_what: A recurring, calendared source of large-area navigation denial inside US airspace — a known annual risk window, not a one-off.

insights.claim: The FAA warned operators ahead of NAVFEST that GPS could be affected up to 400 miles away between May 12 and May 18, meaning the disruption radius was disclosed and anticipated rather than accidental.
insights.speaker: Jeff Wise
insights.so_what: A 400-mile advertised denial footprint inside the continental US quantifies how large the collateral zone of a single exercise is.

insights.claim: Eight minutes after takeoff the crew told Albuquerque Center they had lost GPS and asked for headings, then switched their request from an RNAV approach to an ILS approach because ILS does not require GPS reception.
insights.speaker: Jeff Wise
insights.so_what: Shows ground-based ILS retains value as a jamming-resilient fallback — relevant to any push to decommission legacy navaids.

insights.claim: Air traffic control could not give the crew close attention because three other aircraft simultaneously reported losing GPS and needed help, one struggling to get a bearing on a radio beacon.
insights.speaker: Jeff Wise
insights.so_what: Wide-area jamming creates correlated demand on ATC capacity precisely when individual aircraft need the most help — a systemic, not isolated, failure mode.
insights.locator: In retrospect, tragedy might have been avoided

insights.claim: By 12:08 am the King Air had overshot the landing pattern by 10 miles, and rather than wait for vectors or refly an RNAV approach once GPS returned, the crew requested and was granted a visual approach toward Ruidoso's airport lights 31 miles away.
insights.speaker: Jeff Wise
insights.so_what: The fatal decision came after GPS was restored — the jamming's damage was to crew workload and situational awareness, not just to the signal.
insights.locator: While ATC helped other planes, the King Air continued north

insights.claim: The pilots could not see the 10,000-foot Capitan Mountains across their path, and as the dark rock rose it swiped away the valley lights, which pilot Juan Browne says could have created confusion and a loss of situational awareness.
insights.speaker: Jeff Wise
insights.so_what: The physical failure mode — terrain masking of visual references at night — is what turns a navigation outage into a fatal one.
insights.quote: When those lights go out, man, you know you are in big trouble.

insights.claim: Retired airline pilot Kenneth Krentsa argues the correct response to disorientation is to climb as high as possible and circle in place until position is established, rather than pressing forward blindly as the King Air crew did.
insights.speaker: Jeff Wise
insights.so_what: A trainable procedural fix exists — points to pilot-training and simulator demand as the near-term mitigation market.
insights.quote: You stay in one place until you figure out where you are. You don't just keep pressing forward, blindly.

themes.theme: Compounding risk factors beyond the jamming

insights.claim: Medevac is already among the most dangerous categories of civil aviation, with the law firm Kreindler saying medevac flights have an accident rate more similar to combat flying than to civil aviation.
insights.speaker: Jeff Wise
insights.so_what: Air-medical operators carry combat-grade loss rates — a materially mispriced segment for aviation insurers if EW risk is now additive.
insights.quote: medevac flights have an accident rate more similar to combat flying than to civil aviation
insights.locator: Even absent GPS jamming, medevac is one of the most dangerous

insights.claim: The structural drivers of medevac risk are short-notice dispatch, unfamiliar airstrips and a built-in incentive to fly in marginal weather because human lives are at stake.
insights.speaker: Jeff Wise
insights.so_what: The mission model itself, not equipment, drives the risk — hard to fix with technology alone.
insights.locator: Flights are often organized on short notice

insights.claim: The crew was extraordinarily junior: captain Keelan Clark, 30, had held a commercial license only 18 months and had been promoted from first officer the previous month, while first officer Ali Kawsara, 23, had two months on the job after only cargo work.
insights.speaker: Jeff Wise
insights.so_what: Thin experience in the medevac pilot pool is a compounding variable that jamming exposes — watch crew-experience minimums as a regulatory lever.

insights.claim: The pre-GPS navigation stack — magnetic compasses, ground-based radio beacons and gyroscope-derived inertial systems — requires pilots to build a 3D mental map relative to beacons and demands practiced proficiency to avoid panic and loss of situational awareness.
insights.speaker: Jeff Wise
insights.so_what: Backup navigation is a perishable human skill, not just spare hardware — the industry's real deficit is training hours.

insights.speaker: Jeff Wise
insights.so_what: Environmental conditions determine whether a GPS outage is an inconvenience or a fatality — risk is highly geography- and time-dependent.

themes.theme: Drone warfare is exporting GPS denial into civil airspace

insights.claim: The US military appeared to send out notices for at least 10 GPS jamming exercises in the past year, making the Ruidoso event one instance of a routine practice rather than an anomaly.
insights.speaker: Jeff Wise
insights.so_what: A quantified cadence of domestic navigation-denial events — the exposure is recurring and forecastable.

insights.claim: Cheap, numerous, hard-to-spot drones let smaller, less-resourced nations level the playing field against more powerful adversaries, as Ukraine did against Russia's conventional might after 2022.

insights.so_what: The asymmetry thesis underpins sustained demand for counter-drone and EW spending across many mid-tier militaries.

insights.claim: Because a cheap and simple way for drones to reach targets is GPS, blocking those signals blinds them — but defenders and attackers are locked in an endless cat-and-mouse cycle of countermeasures, which is why exercises like NAVFEST exist.
insights.speaker: Jeff Wise
insights.so_what: Structural, non-terminating arms race implies persistent EW test cadence and therefore persistent civil-aviation spillover.

insights.claim: Since 2023 planes over large swaths of the Middle East, the Black Sea and the Baltic have endured waves of GPS jamming, and while airlines adapt, removing GPS strips away a layer of safety protection even if it does not immediately down aircraft.
insights.speaker: Jeff Wise
insights.so_what: Safety-margin erosion accumulates invisibly until a compounding event — the risk is a step function, not a gradient.

themes.theme: US domestic incidents and a slow-adapting industry

insights.claim: In March 2025 airliners landing at Ronald Reagan National Airport received spurious collision-avoidance alarms and several aborted landings, which turned out to be caused by Secret Service electronic warfare testing at the vice president's residence.
insights.speaker: Jeff Wise
insights.so_what: EW spillover already hits the busiest US political airspace and affects collision avoidance, not just navigation — a broader attack surface than GPS alone.

insights.claim: New Mexico and Texas temporarily closed airspace this year, scaring the public, after US Customs and Border Patrol used anti-drone lasers in the area, and two separate West Texas incidents involving US Army and CBP drone operations disrupted commercial flights.
insights.speaker: Jeff Wise
insights.so_what: Multiple uncoordinated federal agencies are now generating airspace disruption — a coordination failure with no obvious owner.

insights.claim: Todd Humphreys of the University of Texas at Austin argues air travel remains very safe but may be stuck for five years or more in a mild-and-increasing risk situation because the aviation industry is very slow to adapt to growing GPS interference.

insights.claim: Major changes in aviation historically occur only after crashes that kill large numbers of people, and the author predicts a sufficiently motivating catastrophe may not be far off.
